Choose Cedar based on the supplied documentation. It meets both stated requirements: no login and no server retention of prompt text.

The research question is which tool fits those requirements across cost, login, prompt storage, and source access. I compared Fixtures A and B; I did not test either product.

| Criterion | Cedar — Fixture A | Flint — Fixture B |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Unknown; no price stated | Paid plan: USD 8 per month |
| Login requirement | No login required | Account required |
| Prompt storage | Composes prompts locally in the browser; does not send or save prompt text on a server | Sends prompt text to a model API; stores saved prompts on a server; unsaved-prompt retention is unknown |
| Source access | Cannot fetch URLs | Can fetch public web pages |

Cedar fits the required privacy and access conditions, but users must copy prompts into another AI. It cannot retrieve source pages. Flint provides public-page fetching, but its account requirement and server storage of saved prompts conflict with the stated requirements.

These conclusions describe the documentation, not independently verified behavior. Cedar’s price is unknown, so the evidence cannot establish a cost winner. The fixtures do not establish how another AI handles prompts copied from Cedar.

Flint’s “10x better answers” claim has no supporting test results in Fixture B. It does not establish a measured quality advantage.

The abstract does not establish that the diagram lesson is ready for broad adoption. My recommendation is a limited evaluation in the intended setting.

**Question and method**

The study asks whether a short diagram lesson improves immediate assessment scores compared with a text lesson.

Forty volunteers were randomly assigned to two groups, with 20 participants per group. One group received the diagram lesson; the other received the text lesson. Both completed an immediate assessment containing 10 questions.

**Results and uncertainty**

The diagram group averaged 7.0 correct answers. The text group averaged 6.5. The estimated difference was 0.5 points, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.3, 1.3].

The estimated difference favors the diagram lesson. However, the confidence interval spans a 0.3-point disadvantage through a 1.3-point advantage, including no difference. The evidence does not establish a clear improvement or equivalence.

**Limits for adoption**

Random assignment strengthens the comparison within this sample. However, one lesson and one convenience sample limit generalization to other lessons, learners, and settings.

There was no delayed test, so the study does not establish a retention benefit. No completion-time data were collected, so it does not support claims about speed or time savings.

For an adoption decision, define the minimum useful improvement. Evaluate the intervention with the intended learners and lessons, and include a delayed assessment. Collect completion-time data if efficiency matters.

That recommendation is an inference from the study’s uncertainty and limited scope. The abstract reports an uncertain immediate score difference; it does not report evidence of durable or faster learning.
